title: Maxine Paredes
text: Hi! I’m Maxine and I’m originally from Calgary, AB. I completed my BSc in Cognitive Systems and a Minor in Data Science at UBC. Before starting this program, I was a 2025 DSSG Fellow at the UBC Data Science Institute and working as an HRIS Data Analyst at MNP. From the UBC MDS program, I am hoping to gain technical depth and a more holistic understanding of the field to become a Data Scientist.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
First day of school!


We are now in our second week of the MDS program and I have been enjoying my time so far. While it holds up to its reputation as an accelerated program, I feel supported by the teaching team and am already learning so much.
Even in the short amount of time I have been in the program, I can see that immersion and consistency will play a large role in success. The different ways of exposure to new material allows us to both solidfy our understand and identify areas of improvement from various angles.
The immediate volume of work took me by surprise but I am also impressed by the amount of resources that are available to me. I am still trying to find the balance between school, relationships, health and wellness, clubs, and research but I am so excited for the opportunity to grow and build my skills.

title: R: Visualizing the palmerpenguins Dataset
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)


missing_values <- penguins |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing")

missing_values

# A tibble: 8 × 2
  variable          n_missing
  <chr>                 <int>
1 species                   0
2 island                    0
3 bill_length_mm            2
4 bill_depth_mm             2
5 flipper_length_mm         2
6 body_mass_g               2
7 sex                      11
8 year                      0


Before doing any exploratory data analysis, I loaded in the tidyverse and palmerpenguins libraries. I then created a tibble showing the number of missing values in each column of the penguins dataset. I thought that checking for missing data would help identify any gaps in the data can quietly affect summaries and plots later on. For the most part, columns had non-NA values but sex has 11 missing values, and there are 2 penguins that are missing all of their body measurements. Because of this, I use drop_na() in later steps to remove incomplete rows before calculating averages.

missing_sex <- penguins |>
  count(species, missing = is.na(sex)) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  mutate(total = sum(n),
         percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(missing)     

missing_sex

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  species missing     n total percent
  <fct>   <lgl>   <int> <int>   <dbl>
1 Adelie  TRUE        6   152     3.9
2 Gentoo  TRUE        5   124     4  


I wanted to understand which penguin species were missing values for sex and how much of the data was missing relative to each species. The Adelie species is missing 6 records, accounting for 3.9% of Adelie penguins, while Gentoo is missing 5, accounting for 4.0% of Gentoo penguins. Although Adelie has more missing records, the proportions are nearly identical because Adelie has more penguins overall. Chinstrap does not appear in the missing_sex tibble, which indicates that no Chinstrap records are missing sex. Overall, only 11 of 344 penguins (about 3.2%) are missing sex, so the missing values are unlikely to have a large effect on comparisons between males and females.

mean_bill_length_mm <- penguins |>
    drop_na() |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  summarise(average_bill_length = mean(bill_length_mm))


mean_bill_length_mm |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = average_bill_length, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Average bill length by species and sex",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Average bill length (mm)",
    fill = "Sex"
  )







Figure 1: Average Bill Length by Sex and Species





After visualizing the average bill_length_mm by species and sex, we can see that for all three species (Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo), the average bill length of female penguins is consistently shorter than that of male penguins. In addition, Adelie penguins have the shortest bills overall, while Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins have comparable average bill lengths when accounting for sex.

title: About
text:
I graduated with my BSc in Cognitive Systems with a Minor in Data Science from UBC. Throughout my undergrad I worked in multiple research labs across UBC, where I gained experience applying data-driven approaches to investigate questions in social psychology, cognitive science, and sports biomechanics.
In the summer of 2025, I was selected as one of eight individuals for the UBC Data Science Institute’s Data Science for Social Good (DSSG) Program. We partnered with Mentor Canada, the largest non-profit dedicated to expanding access to youth mentorship nationally, to support an upcoming grant application by analyzing survey data to better understand the current landscape of youth mentorship in Canada. Alongside this analysis, I independently designed and implemented a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system to streamline Mentor Canada’s research workflow, enabling the organization to more efficiently access insights from their existing documents.
Following my undergraduate studies, I joined MNP as a Data Analyst in Human Capital. My work involved developing reports and dashboards, analyzing workforce data, and finding ways to improve data usage and management. Moving into industry gave me a new perspective on working with data and helped me understand how analysis can be translated into meaningful insights for organizational decision-making.
Currently, I am completing my MSc in Data Science at UBC where I am expanding my technical foundation and broadening my experience across different areas of data science.

title: About
text:
Why Data Science?
I first became interested in data science when I realized that data is all around us, often in ways we do not immediately recognize. This made me curious about the different ways data can be harnessed to better understand a given field and uncover insights that might otherwise go unnoticed.
I am drawn to data science because it gives me the opportunity to act as a bridge between raw data and meaningful conclusions. I enjoy looking beyond what the data shows to understand why something is the way it is, and translating those findings into conclusions that are accessible and useful to others.
